newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq oil deal up for renewal; US still skeptical.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil deal up for renewal; US still skeptical.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson on Thursday voiced misgivings about the $2 billion oil-for-food deal for Iraq, due for renewal next month.
Richardson did not reject approval for the plan for another six months but indicated Washington was getting ready to demand changes in the distribution of humanitarian goods.

"We are not in a position to say Iraq and the United Nations have implemented the resolution as it was intended. We expected the operation to be far more transparent than it has proven to be in practice," he said.
"The United States government has not yet decided whether to support the extension," he added.

At issue is an accord that went into effect on Dec. 10 and allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months in order to purchase food, medicine and other goods for its people suffering under U.N. sanctions imposed when Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990.

Richardson, the chief U.S. delegate to the United Nations, said Washington needed more information on "Iraq's distribution methods and the means by which the U.N. is monitoring the distribution" as well as the implementation of the programme in the Kurdish-dominated north, which receives a separate allocation.
He also said there would be no rise in oil sales as Iraq had suggested. "You should not expect us to agree on an increase in the volume of oil sales," he said.
U.N. offlicials have said they expected Secretary-General Kofi Annan to recommend $2 billion to the Security Council on similar terms to the present programme.

Richardson's views contrasted with a positive report from Undersecretary-General Yasushi Akashi, whose Department of Humanitarian Affairs is responsible for monitoring the distribution of food, medicine and other goods.

After a briefing by Akashi, Council President Park Soo Gil of South Korea said members "noted that Iraqi authorities are generally cooperative with monitoring activities with the Department of Humanitarian Affairs."

Iraq's key negotiator for the scheme, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, based in Paris, said last month that Baghdad needed at least $4 billion in oil revenues to meet its needs. He also proposed that a week or two be allocated to settling the pending orders for humanitarian supplies.
Iraq has complained frequently that Washington has prevented the supplies from reaching the country within a reasonable period of time while oil sales moved quickly.

Richardson contended that U.S. objections to individual contracts were not politically motivated. He said the contracts it had "put on hold" were due either to improper procedures or concerned items not on the distribution list.
